section_summary: This section covers U.S. State Department records from late 1933 to early 1934 regarding Japanese internal political developments, foreign relations, and economic conditions. It includes the concluding portion of the Tokyo Embassy's monthly report for October 1933 (Report No. 85), internal State Department memoranda evaluating reports, and monthly reports for November 1933 (Report No. 86, Despatch 607) and December 1933 (Report No. 87, Despatch 636). Major topics addressed include Japanese reactions to U.S. diplomatic recognition of the Soviet Union, military budget demands and cabinet friction, reactionary political trials (May 15 incident, God-Sent Troops), disputes over the London Naval Treaty, and evolving Japanese policy toward Manchukuo and China.

subfiles.about: Embassy monthly report reviewing Japanese internal politics, foreign relations, military budget controversies, assassination trials, and economic conditions during October 1933.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This document comprises the concluding pages of the Tokyo Embassy's monthly report for October 1933 along with lists of despatches and telegrams sent during that month. It covers Japanese trade relations with Central and South America, Poland, and Afghanistan, as well as the 'Five Ministers' Conferences' addressing heavy military budget demands from War Minister Sadao Araki. It also details the trials of civilian and naval conspirators from the May 15, 1932 assassination of Premier Inukai, investigations into the 'God-Sent Troops' plot, Communist arrests, controversy over the London Naval Treaty defended by Baron Wakatsuki, and national financial and commodity conditions.
subfiles.title: Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan for October 1933 (Report No. 85, Despatch No. 580)

subfiles.about: Internal State Department memorandum summarizing and analyzing the Tokyo Embassy's monthly political report for November 1933.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: This memorandum analyzes Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 607 (Report No. 86) covering November 1933. It highlights Japanese reactions to U.S. recognition of the Soviet Union, the temporary transfer of the U.S. fleet from the Pacific to the Atlantic, and Soviet-Japanese frictions over alleged airspace violations and the Chinese Eastern Railway. It also examines the Fukien rebellion in China, Manchukuo border annexations, the 1934-1935 draft Japanese budget, and indications of a downward trend in Japanese export trade.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo's November 1933 Report (Despatch No. 607)
subfiles.to: Officers of the Department of State

subfiles.about: Monthly diplomatic report covering Japanese domestic affairs, foreign relations, military trials, budget adoption, and economic developments during November 1933.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 607 transmits Report No. 86 on conditions in Japan for November 1933, complete with a table of contents and lists of Embassy despatches and telegrams. The report reviews the calm but watchful Japanese response to U.S. recognition of the USSR, the positive reaction to the U.S. fleet's movement to the Atlantic, and informal meetings between Ambassador Grew and Foreign Minister Koki Hirota. It also covers the visit of Manuel Quezon, the Fukien rebellion in China, Indo-Japanese trade talks in New Delhi, Kwantung Army plans for the South Manchuria Railway, light sentences handed down to May 15 naval assassins, the attempted assassination of Baron Wakatsuki by an anti-treaty fanatic, adoption of a record 2.11-billion-yen budget, and the death of Princess Nobuko Asaka.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 607: Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan during the Month of November, 1933 (Report No. 86)

subfiles.about: Internal State Department memorandum summarizing significant points in the Tokyo Embassy's monthly report for December 1933.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: This memorandum reviews the Tokyo Embassy's report for December 1933, drawing attention to key diplomatic, political, and economic developments. It notes the appointment of Hiroshi Saito as Ambassador to Washington, Viscount Kikujiro Ishii's conciliatory shift in attitude toward the United States, and suggestions for radio broadcasts to improve bilateral relations. It also notes improving Sino-Japanese trade, the abandonment of Kwantung Army schemes to control the South Manchuria Railway due to Overseas Ministry opposition, growing political and press criticism of the military, and the creation of a foreign affairs advisory planning board headed by Kensuke Horinouchi.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo's December 1933 Report
subfiles.to: Officers of the Department of State

subfiles.about: Monthly diplomatic report covering Japanese political, foreign, and economic relations during December 1933, including U.S. relations, Manchukuo, China, and the Soviet Union.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 636 transmits Report No. 87 on conditions in Japan for December 1933, opening with an index and covering the first half of the report. Major topics discussed include the appointment of Hiroshi Saito as Ambassador to the United States succeeding Katsuji Debuchi, Viscount Ishii's speeches praising U.S.-Japanese commercial interdependence, and goodwill radio exchanges celebrating the birth of the Crown Prince. In foreign affairs, it reviews Japanese concerns over the Fukien rebellion and rumors regarding Golden Gate Island near Amoy, the conclusion of Indo-Japanese trade negotiations at New Delhi, plans to enthroned Henry Pu-Yi as Emperor of Manchukuo on its second anniversary, deadlock over the Chinese Eastern Railway sale, and Soviet border defense works.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 636: Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of December, 1933 (Report No. 87)
